speakeroldname: Hon. W. G. Dinsdale (Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources):
speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
subtopic: FEDERAL PARTICIPA- TION IN CONTROL MEASURES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like, through you, to inform the house of negotiations now proceeding with the province of Ontario for federal support of flood control measures in the metro Toronto region.
Hon. members will be aware that in 1960 the Ontario government asked us to participate in the metro Toronto and region conservation authority plan for the construction of dams, reservoirs, and channel improvements along the Humber and Don rivers and Black creek. The proposal also involves the use of flood-plain lands for flood control and recreation along five other streams, Etobicoke, Duffin, Highland and Mimico creeks, and the Rouge river.
It is expected that an agreement will shortly be signed under the Canada Water Conservation Assistance Act. Under this agreement the federal government would contribute up to 37J per cent of the estimated $24 million capital cost of the works. The government of Ontario would contribute a like amount, and the municipalities in the conservation authority the remaining 25 per cent. The plan will also involve the acquisition or zoning of flood-plain lands for flood control and recreation purposes. To use these lands for recreation will require further works amounting to about $2.6 million, which will be met from sources other than the federal government.
The part of the plan affecting Black creek is now fully engineered, and tenders can be called just as soon as the agreement is concluded. These works will cost in total about $4 million, including almost $900,000 which has already been spent by the authority with the assistance of the government of Ontario on a 50-50 cost sharing basis. These works are designed to prevent the recurrence of flood disasters such as the one caused by
hurricane Hazel which claimed 81 lives in 1954. The works will also have very important secondary benefits in recreation and in providing a regulated water system.

subtopic: FEDERAL PARTICIPA- TION IN CONTROL MEASURES
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, on behalf of the Liberal party I would like to say that we welcome this announcement on the part of the minister. This rather wide-scale scheme has been under consideration for a long period of time now and it is welcome news that a decision has been taken. With the development of this extended conservation region there will be, as the minister has told us, considerable benefit to the inhabitants of the region. Not only from the standpoint of conserving valuable natural resources but also in limiting the damage which may be done in future from floods and at the same time providing outstanding recreational facilities to the inhabitants for many miles around. We say thank you to the minister for having finally reached a decision, and we hope the works will proceed without any further undue delay.

With regard to part 1 of the question, it should be first pointed out that standard time comes exclusively under provincial jurisdiction and therefore is not a subject for consideration by the federal government. However, the question was referred to the railway association of Canada, who advise that from time to time representations are made that the railways should adopt daylight saving time, and that these requests are given careful consideration.

Starred Questions
As to part 2, the railway association does not consider that the adoption of daylight saving time would be workable. The practice is not uniform throughout Canada, there being some provinces, and communities within provinces, which do not put it into effect, and the association also points out that in the operation of trains requiring interchange with United States railways, which operate on standard time, it is essential in the interests of safety that Canadian trains be operated on the same basis. However, before changing the timetables each year to coincide with the adoption of daylight saving time, the association consults with the provinces and the larger municipalities in an endeavour to provide schedules which will meet the convenience of the majority of passengers.
Part 3 is answered by the answer to part 1.

speechtext: Can the Prime Minister give the house any information on the situation in Cuba?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Prime Minister):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in so far as the military situation is concerned, there is nothing to add to that which has appeared in the press. During the past two days official means of communication have been interrupted and it has not been possible for the Canadian embassy to communicate with the government since about noon on Monday. For the same reason we are unable to give any information respecting the safety and well-being of Canadian citizens in Cuba.
The Canadian government is following events in Cuba with much anxiety and deep concern. The struggle between the contending groups has taken on a new and more threatening aspect with the dispatch by Chairman Khrushchev of a message which revealed beyond doubt the extent to which international communism is prepared to go in consolidating its foothold in Cuba, a bridgehead from which the penetration of the whole of Latin America could be launched.
It is now all too clear that the situation in Cuba is much more than a continuation
Inquiries of the Ministry of the original internal revolution which was to a large extent an expression of the legitimate social and economic aspirations of the Cuban people. Cuba, like so many small and defenceless countries, has become the focal point in the ideological contest which is progressively reaching into every corner of the world. In our country we cannot be indifferent to this new danger which affects the hemisphere in which we live.
Cuba is a casualty of the internationalization of its original revolution. In this process the interests of the Cuban people have been subordinated to the interplay of outside forces beyond their control. Civil liberties are further curtailed in the name of national security, and arbitrary acts of reprisal have become a substitute for justice. These are manifestations of a dictatorship which are abhorrent to free men everywhere.
Any threat to the peace of this hemisphere affects us here in Canada. We have neither the means nor the intention to intervene. What we earnestly wish to see established are stable conditions within Cuba which will allow it to develop in peace and live free from outside pressures as a constructive partner of the nations of the western hemisphere.
As the Leader of the Opposition knows, the matter is before the United Nations. Seven Latin American countries have proposed a resolution to bring about the restoration of peaceful relations at the earliest possible date through placing the matter in its various aspects before the organization of American states.

Mr. Speaker, arising out of the Prime Minister's reply, which we appreciate, I should like to ask a supplementary question. In view of the anxiety and concern expressed in Canada, Great Britain, South America and elsewhere over the threat to world peace of the present situation in Cuba, will the government use every means at its disposal to impress upon the government of the United States the immediate necessity of doing what is possible to promote peace in that area, and of utilizing the United Nations to assist and promote the development of democratic institutions and the stability of the Cuban economy?

Mr. Speaker, there is very little I can add to what I have already said. I might say, however, that this morning the Secretary of State for External Affairs had a meeting with Mr. Adlai Stevenson, the United States ambassador to the United Nations, and discussed this matter in all its ramifications and effects. I think I cannot go any further.

speechtext: The house resumed, from Tuesday, April 18, consideration of the motion of Mr. Fleming (Eglinton) for the second reading of Bill No. C-82, to implement a convention between Canada and the United States of America for the avoidance of double taxation and the prevention of fiscal evasion with respect to taxes on the estates of deceased persons.

subtopic: CONVENTION BETWEEN CANADA AND UNITED STATES FOR AVOIDANCE OF DOUBLE TAXATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we are now on second reading of a bill with respect to a tax agreement by treaty with the United States for the avoidance of double taxation. As I understand it, this agreement results from an attempt by Canada, and other countries with which Canada is in close touch in these matters, to avoid double taxation. Of course, I understand that the rather radical revision of our law with respect to estates of deceased persons in 1958 made this agreement necessary. We even changed our terminology from succession duty act to estates tax.
Hon. members in assembly here will recognize that the effective date of the new policy was to be January 1, 1959. Before the debate is concluded I would hope that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) would indicate to us all what the effect has been since January 1, 1959, and the enactment of this law relating to estates that are dealt with in the legislation before us. Under the old provisions which many members of this house discussed in 1958 in the banking and commerce committee under the chairmanship of the hon. member for York North (Mr. Cathers), we 90205-6-240i
Estate Tax
then were aware that $5,000 of estate was exempt from taxation on both sides of the border if owned by a decedent on either side of the border. However, I believe this was a disappearing exemption to the extent that, if it was $6,000 in ownership in a country other than the residence of the decedent- Canada or the United States and vice versa- a tax was applicable on the whole amount of the estate.
I do not think that situation is changed under this tax treaty. However, as I understand it-and I hope the minister will inform me and the country about this matter-instead of what we talked about in the committee of banking and commerce in 1958 as a $5,000 fundamental exemption, we now have here before us a $15,000 fundamental exemption. In other words, if a Canadian resident has assets in the United States valued at $15,000 at his death, there would be no tax payable in the United States on those assets; and vice versa, if a resident of the United States had assets in Canada valued at less than $15,000, under the treaty there would be no tax payable on those assets in Canada. I should like to hear the minister say something about that matter in order to see whether it confirms the conception we have on this side of the house. I understand that hitherto, in the assessment of an estate, charitable deductions-even charitable deductions of a kind that would be recognized for tax deduction in this country-would not in the case of a United States resident have been recognized for deduction if the charity was one operating in the United States. Perhaps the minister would confirm that understanding. He may have made that matter clear in his statement on February 17th.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: CONVENTION BETWEEN CANADA AND UNITED STATES FOR AVOIDANCE OF DOUBLE TAXATION
speechtext: Yes; I dealt with it in that statement.

Apart from that, I think there is very little disagreement about the desirability of extending, as widely and as rapidly as we can do so, tax agreements with other friendly countries which make it possible for business to be conducted or for assets to be taken over in countries other than the country of residence and to assure that there will not be double taxation of estates after death.
I have personally received no complaint with respect to this particular bill and the negotiations that have resulted since we changed our estate law in 1958. I should like the minister to make some comment as to what happens between January 1, 1959, and the enactment of the present law in so far as the present bill varies the formerly existing legislation passed as a result of the former treaty.

The hon. member asked about the position of charitable organizations under the bill. I did deal with this matter in my statement to the house on February 17. The particular matter was touched on at page 2146 of Hansard.
I may say that article III, paragraph 2 of the convention does contain a new feature in this regard. In other words the international border, for this purpose, is now being ignored.
This provision is reciprocal and will bring Canadian practice into line with long standing United States' practice. It will, of course, be beneficial to the estates of Canadian domi-ciliaries where a bequest of this kind has been made.

subtopic: CONVENTION BETWEEN CANADA AND UNITED STATES FOR AVOIDANCE OF DOUBLE TAXATION
speechtext: No, Mr. Chairman.

subtopic: CONVENTION BETWEEN CANADA AND UNITED STATES FOR AVOIDANCE OF DOUBLE TAXATION
speechtext: Am I correct in thinking that with respect to the revision of our law in 1958 regarding taxation on estates of deceased persons, under other tax treaties with most countries across the world no legislative revision was necessary, but there is something in the United States-Canadian tax treaty that makes this bill imperative and necessary?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: CONVENTION BETWEEN CANADA AND UNITED STATES FOR AVOIDANCE OF DOUBLE TAXATION
speechtext: Yes, Mr. Chairman, having regard to the purposes of the legislation.

subtopic: CONVENTION BETWEEN CANADA AND UNITED STATES FOR AVOIDANCE OF DOUBLE TAXATION
speechtext:
With respect to mutual agreement by conventions between Canada and other countries, with what other countries have we tax agreements that will not involve, as are involved here, legislative changes because of what this parliament did in 1958 when it radically revised our estates tax system?
With how many countries have we conventions with respect to the avoidance of double taxation that have not, because of their context, required any parliamentary review since 1958, such as is required here?
I ask this question because I understand that the agreement with the United States was tied in fairly definitely with the dominion succession duty act, which was abolished by the action of this parliament in 1958.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: CONVENTION BETWEEN CANADA AND UNITED STATES FOR AVOIDANCE OF DOUBLE TAXATION
speechtext:
As I pointed out last night in introducing the motion for second reading, Canada has at the present time conventions with the United Kingdom, France, Ireland and South Africa as well as the 1944 convention with the United States.
The 1944 convention was the first of these conventions that Canada entered into with another country with respect to the avoidance of double taxation, and it related specifically to the dominion succession duty act.
The later conventions with the other four countries were broader in their terms and also took account of similar legislation. Consequently no amendment is required in the

conventions with the four countries I have named, and the enactment of the Estate Tax Act has resulted accordingly only in the revision of the convention with the United States.

subtopic: CONVENTION BETWEEN CANADA AND UNITED STATES FOR AVOIDANCE OF DOUBLE TAXATION
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, as I understand it this particular convention supersedes anything in the Estate Tax Act that is inconsistent with legislation in the United States.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: CONVENTION BETWEEN CANADA AND UNITED STATES FOR AVOIDANCE OF DOUBLE TAXATION
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, this present convention, if given legislative sanction by parliament, will supersede any provision in the Estate Tax Act which is inconsistent with the terms of the convention.

subtopic: CONVENTION BETWEEN CANADA AND UNITED STATES FOR AVOIDANCE OF DOUBLE TAXATION
speechtext: With what we are enacting today?

subtopic: CONVENTION BETWEEN CANADA AND UNITED STATES FOR AVOIDANCE OF DOUBLE TAXATION
speechtext: That was the point I had in mind, because the Estate Tax Act, unwittingly I am sure as far as the minister and the house are concerned, failed to take account of the situation that confronted many taxpayers in the United States who have property in Canada. I think the minister will find that this is right.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: CONVENTION BETWEEN CANADA AND UNITED STATES FOR AVOIDANCE OF DOUBLE TAXATION
speechtext:
I can assure the hon. member that this was not overlooked. It was well understood at the time.
In the banking and commerce committee, I think it was, when the bill which later became the Estate Tax Act was under review, this matter was discussed and mention was made of the intention of the government to negotiate a further convention with the United States which would take account of the change in the situation brought about by the enactment of the Estate Tax Act.

subtopic: CONVENTION BETWEEN CANADA AND UNITED STATES FOR AVOIDANCE OF DOUBLE TAXATION
speechtext:
But the fault was not because of an agreement between Canada and the United States. For instance, if the full implications of the treaty of 1944 had been followed the omission in the Estate Tax Act would not have occurred.
This was a matter of very great concern to my section of the country, adjacent as it is to the United States, where thousands of people have property along the great lakes, which they use during the summer months. They are a source of considerable income to southwestern Ontario. I am sure this situation applies to many other parts of Canada.
Now the matter is to be corrected, and this is of course welcomed. However, it seems to me there has been a very long delay in arriving at a culmination of the negotiations-

subtopic: CONVENTION BETWEEN CANADA AND UNITED STATES FOR AVOIDANCE OF DOUBLE TAXATION
speechtext: Since 1958.

subtopic: CONVENTION BETWEEN CANADA AND UNITED STATES FOR AVOIDANCE OF DOUBLE TAXATION
speechtext:
-since 1958. I recall asking the minister a number of times when we might expect some finality between the two governments with respect to this
Estate Tax
matter. Although on one occasion I got from the minister some correspondence which was encouraging, I was never able to elicit from him in the house anything which was correspondingly optimistic.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: CONVENTION BETWEEN CANADA AND UNITED STATES FOR AVOIDANCE OF DOUBLE TAXATION
speechtext: You should stick to correspondence. That is the moral.

subtopic: CONVENTION BETWEEN CANADA AND UNITED STATES FOR AVOIDANCE OF DOUBLE TAXATION
speechtext:
That may be true. If the subsequent acts of the minister were consistent with the correspondence, that observation would be very pertinent. But that was not the situation.
There must be some reason why there has been this long delay since 1958. My reason for making these observations arises from concern over the situation which affected thousands of people in southwestern Ontario as well as in other parts of Canada and in the United States. What were the reasons for the delay in reaching a successful outcome of these negotiations? It was said at one meeting of the tax foundation by a distinguished lawyer that the Canadian negotiators were dilatory. I do not know that it was said that the minister was dilatory, but the minister must accept responsibility for any delay on the part of the negotiating team. In any event, there was a long delay from the time these discussions began. The minister first gave us an assurance that this matter would be dealt with at an early date, and I should like the hon. gentleman to explain now why the delay has been so protracted. Was it because he himself was so preoccupied that he was not able to give instructions to our negotiators, or was it the fault of the other side? In any event there has been widespread criticism of the government's failure to act constructively and rapidly with regard to these negotiations and in these circumstances I think some explanation should be given.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: CONVENTION BETWEEN CANADA AND UNITED STATES FOR AVOIDANCE OF DOUBLE TAXATION
speechtext:
There has been no delay and no dilatoriness. Negotiations with the United States with a view to such a convention as is now before the committee began in September 1958, just after the Estate Tax Act was enacted and before the proclamation of that act brought it into effect. The negotiations proved difficult, but they were completed, as the convention indicates, and signed on February 17 of this year. That is not an unusual length of time to require for negotiations with respect to such a tax agreement as this. If the hon. gentleman would look back to the days when he was a minister he might recall that negotiations between Canada and other countries with respect to similar conventions very often occupied two years.

Estate Tax

subtopic: CONVENTION BETWEEN CANADA AND UNITED STATES FOR AVOIDANCE OF DOUBLE TAXATION
speechtext:
May I just say I have had some correspondence in connection with this matter, not only with the minister but with others, over the difficulties which arose through failure to arrive at an earlier understanding with the United States authorities. As of January 1, 1959, we know that the tax convention between the United States and Canada with regard to the elimination of double succession duties had ceased to exist. The reason, of course, was that the former treaty, the treaty conceived and executed in 1944, applied only in the case of the dominion succession duty act which was superseded by the Estate Tax Act. I had asked the minister in the house what was the nature of the negotiations which were under way and if there was any reason to expect an early settlement of the matter. The minister replied in the house-I do not have the exact reference to Hansard-that that was the case.
Subsequently, I had some correspondence with one of the departmental officials as late as March 16, 1959. I was told then that a tax convention was being negotiated but that the negotiations were not then complete. I believe the minister said I had had some experience in these matters-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: CONVENTION BETWEEN CANADA AND UNITED STATES FOR AVOIDANCE OF DOUBLE TAXATION
speechtext:
I did not say the
hon. gentleman had had experience in these particular matters.

subtopic: CONVENTION BETWEEN CANADA AND UNITED STATES FOR AVOIDANCE OF DOUBLE TAXATION
speechtext: I thought the minister said I was a member of the government, and I assumed that was what he meant. Well, I have had some experience with negotiations, though not on behalf of the Department of Finance, and I do not believe the minister has given us a satisfactory reply as to why there has been this long waiting period. This delay has had some consequences of serious account to us in ssex county. Some withdrawals have taken place -not as many, perhaps, as one would have anticipated, but nevertheless there have been some. It is hard to explain why results should not have been achieved more quickly, particularly since we have had a pattern treaty since 1944 and other treaties with other countries, including France, as the minister mentioned last night in his statement of explanation which appears in Hansard. However. I can do no more than say it does seem to me there has not yet been a satisfactory explanation given of the delay in bringing about a settlement of matters leading to this convention.

subtopic: CONVENTION BETWEEN CANADA AND UNITED STATES FOR AVOIDANCE OF DOUBLE TAXATION
speechtext:
I should like to ask the minister what has happened to the processing of involved estates from January 1, 1959, up until today or, at least, until the signing of the convention. Perhaps I might also ask

another question. As reported on page 2145 of Hansard the minister said the taxes included in the scope of the new convention are the Canadian estate tax, the United States estate tax and other taxes of a substantially similar character. I should like to know what those other taxes are.
Further on in his remarks, the minister said:
However, the United States which uses a schedule of graduated rates, is not obliged to restrict its rates; instead it is required to allow a deductible exemption of $2,000 in all cases where the property is valued at more than $15,000.
I wonder if, in that particular case, that would be advantageous to Canada or not.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: CONVENTION BETWEEN CANADA AND UNITED STATES FOR AVOIDANCE OF DOUBLE TAXATION
speechtext:
The dominion succession duty act is still in effect. No doubt it will be in effect for a long time to come. It is still the legislation which governs the tax for federal purposes on estates of persons who died in Canada before January 1, 1959. The Estate Tax Act applies only to the estates of persons dying on or after January 1, 1959. So, as to what has happened since January 1, 1959, I may say that with respect to the estates of persons who died before January 1, 1959, their cases are still dealt with under the dominion succession duty act and so far as the United States property is concerned they are still governed by the convention of 1944 and will continue to be so. As to what has happened since January 1, 1959, with respect to estates of persons who died on or after January 1, 1959, I may say that these cases have not been closed pending the negotiation of this convention, and wide publicity was given to the fact that these negotiations were being carried on.
As I mentioned earlier, when the bill respecting the estate tax was before parliament at the 1958 session, it was made known that it was the government's intention to undertake negotiations with the United States with a view to a new convention applicable to the estates of persons dying on or after January 1, 1959. If this bill is passed, the final clause of the convention provides that the convention shall be deemed to have come into effect and been applicable from January 1, 1959.

subtopic: CONVENTION BETWEEN CANADA AND UNITED STATES FOR AVOIDANCE OF DOUBLE TAXATION
speechtext:
I should like to get from the minister some direct clarification of my own understanding of this bill. In the riding which I represent there are several large corporations, which are subsidiaries of United States companies, whose employees are allowed to purchase stock during their working years. Recently, we have had problems arising from the fact an estate was faced with double taxation in connection with the stock because it was United States stock. Will

the passage of this bill eliminate those problems-of course, subject to the amount of stock held in U.S.A. being not over $15,000.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: CONVENTION BETWEEN CANADA AND UNITED STATES FOR AVOIDANCE OF DOUBLE TAXATION
speechtext: It would be very difficult for me to give a definite answer to a question of that kind without having a great deal more information about the circumstances of the individual case about which the hon. member is inquiring. I may say in general terms, however, that the purpose of the present measure is to avoid double taxation; that is, as between Canada and the United States. The specific terms of this convention would have to be examined with respect to the particular facts of each case to determine the result; but the purpose of the convention is to avoid double taxation, and that is its effect within the terms of the convention.

subtopic: CONVENTION BETWEEN CANADA AND UNITED STATES FOR AVOIDANCE OF DOUBLE TAXATION
speechtext: As the minister said when he spoke just a few moments ago, the result is that this bill provides for a retroactive feature, but as of what date?

subtopic: CONVENTION BETWEEN CANADA AND UNITED STATES FOR AVOIDANCE OF DOUBLE TAXATION
speechtext: January 1, 1959.

subtopic: CONVENTION BETWEEN CANADA AND UNITED STATES FOR AVOIDANCE OF DOUBLE TAXATION
speechtext: This legislation comes into effect as of that date; in other words, the retroactivity goes back to that date? What is the situation in respect of estates which have been disposed of in the meantime, where the amount owing to the crown or to the people of the United States has been agreed on? What is the position of the beneficiaries of the estate or of anyone in any way affected by the estate with regard to the settlement made, say, within the last 12 months?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: CONVENTION BETWEEN CANADA AND UNITED STATES FOR AVOIDANCE OF DOUBLE TAXATION
speechtext: These will all be adjusted on application in accordance with the terms of the new convention.

subtopic: CONVENTION BETWEEN CANADA AND UNITED STATES FOR AVOIDANCE OF DOUBLE TAXATION
speechtext: I have two questions to ask the minister. Will the minister explain to the committee the difference between a treaty and a convention? Does one have to do with water and the other with money? Second, while we realize that this is the usual procedure and practice with respect to arrangements to avoid double taxation between various countries, has any consideration ever been given to an international approach to this question through the United Nations by which there would gradually come a more or less international form and practice with respect to taxation and matters of that kind?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: CONVENTION BETWEEN CANADA AND UNITED STATES FOR AVOIDANCE OF DOUBLE TAXATION
speechtext:
With respect to international agreements, the vogue is to employ the term "convention" where the subject matter of the agreement is taxation or matters of that nature.
As to the second question, I would think it is sufficiently complex now trying to negotiate
Estate Tax
bilateral agreements with other countries in such situations without undertaking a multilateral approach to this type of problem.

subtopic: CONVENTION BETWEEN CANADA AND UNITED STATES FOR AVOIDANCE OF DOUBLE TAXATION
speechtext: I am not suggesting it would be practical at the present time; I only wondered whether there had been any consideration given to an approach, something like that which we have with respect to meteorological services and things of that sort, to get a standard practice, say, throughout the western world?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: CONVENTION BETWEEN CANADA AND UNITED STATES FOR AVOIDANCE OF DOUBLE TAXATION
speechtext: I understand that in one of the committees of O.E.E.C. some consideration was given to this problem, but I think I may suggest to the hon. member that it will not be easy. However, I would not exclude the possibility of study being given to such a question under the auspices of the reconstituted O.E.C.D.

subtopic: CONVENTION BETWEEN CANADA AND UNITED STATES FOR AVOIDANCE OF DOUBLE TAXATION
speechtext: Am I right in thinking that under the radical revision of succession duties made in 1958 with respect to assets of a United States resident with interest in Canada, under no circumstances would the tax be more than 15 per cent of those assets in Canada? If this is so-

speechtext:
Yes. The desire was to have some simplification of these matters. In so far as the convention between Canada and the United States is concerned, we are not on comparable grounds in all respects. For instance, this 15 per cent over-all tax represents our method of assessing our tax on the assets in Canada of a United States domiciled deceased person, but it would not necessarily be the way that a Canadian deceased person's estate would be treated if he had assets in the United States. Will the minister indicate to the committee what the rates of duty might be in the other circumstance? Am I right in thinking that perhaps those rates of duty, depending of course, upon the volume of assets left by the deceased, might range from perhaps 3 per cent to 77 per cent?
I do not recall referring to this matter when I spoke on second reading following the minister. I do not think I referred to the question of whether or not Canada and the United States, as a result of adopting this convention, will be in harmony in the matter of the definitions of situs of property. Perhaps the minister mentioned this on February 17. I am frank to say I have not read his remarks within the last few days. We are not in harmony with respect to tax rates- that is agreed-on the same amount of assets that might be left by a resident of the United

Estate Tax
States in Canada. In our case we have simplified this thing to 15 per cent. With respect to definitions of situs of property, will the minister indicate whether or not we have more or less harmony between the two jurisdictions in this matter?

subtopic: CONVENTION BETWEEN CANADA AND UNITED STATES FOR AVOIDANCE OF DOUBLE TAXATION
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, estate taxes in the two countries are, of course, different. This is one of the features that sometimes make the negotiation of a convention of this kind a very complicated matter. In the Estate Tax Act parliament approved the adoption of the flat 15 per cent tax on Canadian property of persons domiciled abroad.

subtopic: CONVENTION BETWEEN CANADA AND UNITED STATES FOR AVOIDANCE OF DOUBLE TAXATION

subtopic: CONVENTION BETWEEN CANADA AND UNITED STATES FOR AVOIDANCE OF DOUBLE TAXATION

subtopic: CONVENTION BETWEEN CANADA AND UNITED STATES FOR AVOIDANCE OF DOUBLE TAXATION

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: CONVENTION BETWEEN CANADA AND UNITED STATES FOR AVOIDANCE OF DOUBLE TAXATION
speechtext:
We will come to that. The United States federal estate tax, of course, is different. The rates under that tax rise from 3 per cent to a maximum of 77 per cent and there is an exemption of $2,000 in the case of a taxable estate. This is the beginning from which the convention negotiations follow.
Under the new convention, as we will see when we come to the articles, provision is made for a comparable treatment of assets in either case, that is to say, persons domiciled in the United States dying with assets in Canada or persons domiciled in Canada dying with assets in the United States.
With respect to situs, Mr. Chairman, there have been differences in the rules for determination of situs as between the two jurisdictions up to the present time but one of the achievements of this convention is a harmonization of the rules for determination of situs of assets in the two countries for the purposes of this convention.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: CONVENTION BETWEEN CANADA AND UNITED STATES FOR AVOIDANCE OF DOUBLE TAXATION

subtopic: CONVENTION BETWEEN CANADA AND UNITED STATES FOR AVOIDANCE OF DOUBLE TAXATION
speechtext: I must say that I am rather sorry to see this linguistic intrusion from the United States which is further evidence of their influence even upon the statutes of this parliament.

subtopic: CONVENTION BETWEEN CANADA AND UNITED STATES FOR AVOIDANCE OF DOUBLE TAXATION

subtopic: CONVENTION BETWEEN CANADA AND UNITED STATES FOR AVOIDANCE OF DOUBLE TAXATION
speechtext:

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: CONVENTION BETWEEN CANADA AND UNITED STATES FOR AVOIDANCE OF DOUBLE TAXATION

speechtext:
The house resumed from Tuesday, March 14, consideration in committee of the following resolution-Mr. Starr-Mr. Flynn in the chair:
That it is expedient to introduce a measure to authorize the Minister of Labour, with the approval
90205-6-241
Vocational Rehabilitation of the governor in council, to enter into agreements with provinces to provide for the sharing of costs incurred by the provinces in carrying out programs of vocational rehabilitation for disabled persons; to authorize the minister to undertake the co-ordination of federal activities in the field of vocational rehabilitation and to undertake research in respect to vocational rehabilitation; and for those purposes to provide for the establishment of a council to be called the national advisory council on the rehabilitation of disabled persons; and to provide further for the payment of the chairman's remuneration and of the travelling and other expenses of the members thereof and for such professional, technical, secretarial and other assistance as the council may require.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR AGREEMENTS WITH PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in the few minutes at my disposal on March 14, the last opportunity we had to debate this resolution, I was in the process of expressing hope that this particular resolution would amount to something and not just be further window dressing. I think there is need for real effort on the part of all hon. members for progress in this particular field. This is another field where we have seen far too often what I like to describe as one of the greatest national problems, the problem of self-delusion. I should like to give an illustration of what I mean.
In my constituency we have a television station which presents a program each Thursday night between 10.30 and 11 called "Northern Neighbours". This program is sponsored by the local mine managers' association in the Porcupine-Matheson mining district, and is put forward as a public relations effort. One full program on a Thursday evening was devoted to the promotion of the march of dimes. We all realize that the march of dimes is an organization which devotes its efforts, money and resources to alleviating the problems of disabled individuals.
The self-delusion of which I speak is illustrated by the fact that on the very morning of the day that this march of dimes program appeared I received a telephone call from a local doctor who requested me to use my efforts in an attempt to alleviate the distress of a local miner who was forced to stay away from work for a considerable period of time as the result of a heart attack. A heart attack of this kind is a disability, just as a broken leg or back is a disability. The doctor informed me that he felt a rest of four to six months would allow the man to recover without permanent damage and would enable him to return to work. Then, with proper care, he could carry on his duties and provide for himself and his family. The problem that arose was how the man would maintain himself and family for a period of four to six months without being able to work. The miners in that area, as in many other places, have sickness and accident policies which cover them for a limited period

Vocational Rehabilitation of time. At the end of this time the employee must work at least one day in order to reinstate himself for coverage under this policy for an additional period.
The doctor in question, who was familiar with this requirement, against his better judgment, sent the man back to work for the one day required in order to requalify himself. The miner went back to work for one day at which time he was fired by the company. That same night the company, with others, purchased the half-hour of television time devoted to promoting the march of dimes which, as I have said, devotes its energy to the alleviation of the plight of disabled persons.
I feel that example indicates how we have deluded ourselves. I am sure there are many well meaning people in this group who would be horrified if this situation were brought to their attention. I think this is the kind of thing which was in the mind of that great Scottish poet, Robbie Burns, many years ago when he wrote the following:
Oh wad some power the giftie gie us
To see oursels as others see us!
It wad frae monie a blunder free us,
An' foolish notion.
I think in cases like this we should realize that it is not enough to make gestures without carrying out the action to give them some meaning. Unfortunately, we have seen far too much of this type of thing done by the present government. It has made gestures in many directions, many of which have not achieved the intended result. We have seen the government make gestures with regard to a winter works program for the alleviation of the unemployment situation, but in spite of that we have had one of the worst unemployment situations since the Liberal rule in 1938. We have seen the advancement of a vocational training program by this government, but every day there are more individuals thrown out of work than this program can cope with. We have seen this government bring in many patches of legislation directed to our railway problems, yet we received just a week ago the report of a royal commission which shows that in spite of these patches of legislation the situation grows worse. In some instances the report shows clearly that these patches of legislation have aggravated the situation rather than cured it.
The problem we are trying to cope with by this proposed resolution is a very important and urgent one. I appreciate this very much, coming from a riding with heavy industry, industry which has wet, heavy, dusty and unhealthy working conditions. We have a great number of employees in this area who have been disabled through back injuries, silicosis


and various other things. Many of these individuals receive partial pensions, while others receive no pension at all. The individuals receiving pensions are far from able to maintain themselves and their families. I feel it is not good enough for us to say that this is the responsibility of the compensation board, because these are responsibilities which we must accept. While the compensation board is in itself a good organization, it certainly is not capable of solving all the problems of these individuals.
I should like at this time to list six illustrations with which I became familiar last week end when I was at home. I know of one individual who has been off work for some 10 or 11 years on a silicosis pension of $100 per month. He has been attempting to maintain himself and his wife and provide his children with an education. I do not know how he has been able to do so, but at the present time he is in the process of putting his last daughter through teachers' college. He has done so with the $100 per month pension and whatever he could scrape and scrounge in addition.
Silicosis is a very disabling and crippling disease which does not permit an individual to carry on as a normal, healthy individual could.
In another case a former miner, who has been off work now for five years and has been struggling to make ends meet by operating a little country store, is alleged to have a heart condition but he is called in every six months for silicosis X-ray. He has no pension. Here is a man who is disabled and has been in that condition for five years.
There is the case of another man who lives just about a half a mile away, and who has a chest disability. He also has been off work for five years. Apparently he does not qualify for a silicosis pension from the compensation board because the extent of the silicosis has not reached the required percentage.
Another case is that of a young man, 30 years or 31 years of age, who two years ago was crippled in a car accident, has a broken back and will be confined to a wheel chair for the rest of his life. At the present time he is living at Golden Manor, the home for the aged at Timmins. Surely, under this program that is contemplated today, something can be done for people like these.
We have another case of a man who had two feet smashed while working in the bush. He cannot wear proper shoes. He certainly cannot carry on the job he has always done in the bush. He is badly in need of some kind of retraining in order to enable him to make his living and to get by in life with the disability he has.
The final case is that of a chap who suffered from poliomyelitis some years ago, and

who has one bad leg. He also is a bush worker. In the summertime when the ground is firm he can get around. However, as soon as winter comes and he is obliged to pull this crippled leg through the snow, he again is incapacitated.
I am sure that many other hon. members, like myself, have in their files in their offices literally hundreds of cases similar to the ones I have listed here. These were ones that were referred to me on one week end alone or one Saturday alone. I have literally hundreds of similar cases listed in my files. I am sure that other hon. members have at least an equal number and perhaps some of them have more.
This is one of the most serious problems we have to face in this country. The need is desperate in this field. I think we should realize that if some people say the costs involved would be very high, we should stop trying to delude ourselves, and we would find that the costs were not high at all. These costs are being met in any event. They are met or should be met at the present time through municipal welfare, through the assistance of their families and friends and through some other sources. I hope we really are going to take the bull by the horns and do a job in this field of trying to make the disabled people in this country a little better able to fend for themselves and for the communities in which they live.

It gives me great pleasure, Mr. Chairman, to take part in this debate. This resolution which has been brought down by the Minister of Labour has a great deal to commend it, and indeed I am sure it will receive the support of all hon. members. In bringing down this resolution the government, of course, is carrying on the work which is going on throughout the world. I should like to read from the recommendations concerning vocational rehabilitation of the disabled passed at the international labour conference of the international labour organization because I think they contain an important point which we certainly must remember:
Whereas there are many and varied problems concerning those who suffer disability, and
Whereas rehabilitation of such persons is essential in order that they be restored to the fullest possible physical, mental, social, vocational and economic usefulness of which they are capable, and
Whereas to meet the employment needs of the individual disabled person and to use manpower resources to the best advantage it is necessary to develop and restore the working ability of disabled persons by combining into one continuous and co-ordinated process medical, psychological, social, educational, vocational guidance, vocational training and placement services, including follow-up,
The conference recommends as follows:
I should like to read the second recommendation, which is as follows:
90205-6-241i
Vocational Rehabilitation 2. Vocational rehabilitation services should be made available to all disabled persons, whatever the origin and nature of their disability and whatever their age, provided they can be prepared for, and have reasonable prospects of securing and retaining, suitable employment.
I think this is extremely interesting. I wonder whether there has been full recognition, on the part of those drafting this measure, of the fact that simply preparing people through vocational rehabilitation to do a job and then not being able to provide that job can perhaps do more harm than good. I should like to ask this government, which evidently cannot find employment for people who need no rehabilitation and who are not disabled, whether they can promise that they can organize this economy in such a way that such employment can be found for disabled people who have had vocational rehabilitation. I hope so; because if not, what we are doing here today has very little meaning. I repeat that the international labour organization suggests that the disabled be prepared for jobs, provided that they have reasonable prospects of securing and retaining suitable employment.
Vocational rehabilitation has had both a long history and a short history in Canada. We can find this rehabilitation going on through the Department of Veterans Affairs since world war I and workmen's compensation boards in many provinces have been carrying on effective work for many years. Of course, we are reminded constantly of the work of private agencies. Yet, in many ways, Canada is far behind in this program. Prior to 1951 we had no real national vocational rehabilitation program whatsoever. What we had rather was a great mass of agencies, none of them really very well co-ordinated. We have come a long way in ten years, but we have a long way to go. I hope that the particular piece of legislation, which this resolution precedes will be a long stride in that direction and will give effect to the realization that we have to give those who are unfortunately disabled in our country the opportunity which they must have to take part in the economy.
We are reminded by the Department of National Health and Welfare that we are dealing with a considerable number of people in Canada. According to their booklet, over 500,000 people have been seriously or totally disabled. We are also dealing with a great deal of money, namely some $6 million voted by governments across Canada in support of this kind of rehabilitation activity, exclusive of what is being given to the veterans and to the injured through workmen's compensation. In dealing with this resolution which will allow the government to make arrangements with the provinces to share the

Vocational Rehabilitation costs of a larger, more comprehensive and more efficient kind of rehabilitation program, the government is assured of the support of this group. It is assured of that support for humanitarian reasons, of course. In a civilized country, a western democracy, we can do nothing else but do everything in our power to help those who through some misfortune have lost a limb, an eye or have been disabled in some other way. It is not charity. In a sense, it is merely enlightened self-interest.
I was interested in the statistics of the Department of Labour with regard to a group of disabled workmen who were rehabilitated. It was found that whereas previously only 41 were earning over $2,000 per annum, after rehabilitation over 720 were earning over $2,000 a year.
Only 107 of a given group were earning between $1,000 and $2,000 a year. There were 369 after rehabilitation. In other words, there was a considerable rise in the productivity of the individual, in his ability to support himself.
In a sense, what we are doing in passing a resolution of this kind is not really giving charity but simply indicating our interest, and indeed our self-interest, that these people will be able to play a real part in the economy of our nation.
Certainly we can give money to support them, but how much better it is to give them a means of contributing to the society in which they live. A change is indicated even in the kind of work these people are able to undertake. Whereas before rehabilitation only 39 were able to carry out what can be considered professional or managerial occupations, the figure rose to 123 after rehabilitation. The unskilled occupations of course went down from 215 to 94. These men were able to make perhaps an even greater contribution to the economy, as well as being able to support themselves.
Therefore I do not think the effect of vocational rehabilitation can be seriously questioned. However, we do need greater organization. The remarks of the Minister of Labour in introducing his resolution lead me to believe that the national government will give greater leadership to the provincial governments. It will co-ordinate the work of the Department of Health and Welfare, the Department of Labour and the Department of Veterans Affairs, the polio foundation, the Canadian National Institute for the Blind and a great many agencies which are working in this area of vocational rehabilitation.
Unfortunately it could be suggested that in the past there has been too much overlapping; that too many people have been collecting funds and the cost of collecting those funds


has in itself cancelled out the benefit, in a sense, because of course the costs of administration rise as you get several groups trying to obtain the same charity dollar from the individual Canadian. We hope that this overlapping, which has in the past been a disadvantage to rehabilitation, will be eliminated through the implementation of this resolution, and enable a real advancement to be made toward more effective action on the part of these agencies. We know this is essentially a provincial responsibility, but we are beginning to realize-and I hope we have already realized-that there are many things which are outside the resources of the provincial governments.
I hope this resolution will do something in the direction of assuring that those provinces which are less affluent will gain more money and greater opportunities.
We on this side of the house have been rather concerned about the darkening picture of dominion-provincial relations since this government took office. We are a little concerned that we are going back, as one provincial premier said, to the jungle of the 1930's and the 1940's. We certainly hope that equality of opportunity will still be the hallmark of this particular resolution, even if in other areas it appears that the government is going in other directions.
We hope that this equalization will not be eroded, to use a favourite word of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming), any more than it has been by what has happened here in Ottawa in the last three months.
Part of this resolution deals with research in vocational rehabilitation. Job requirements are changing, and it may very well be that the activity in the area of automation will help the problem of those who are disabled and need vocational rehabilitation. As the activities in the physical sense decrease and the areas of mental excellence increase, the physically disabled will certainly have an advantage over what they now have.
However, I am concerned, and I am concerned as much in this area as I am in any other, that this government does not fully recognize what is going to happen. I am concerned that there will not be sufficient research into the whole strata of jobs, where industry is going, what industries are going to play a greater part in the Canadian economy, and what jobs are going to disappear over the next 10 or 20 years as a result of automation.
I hope that when these resolutions are put into effect we will not train disabled people, any more than we will train people who are able to carry on normal job activities, for jobs which will be obsolete within the next five, six or 10 years.

I wish I could see more activity in this area of research. I hope that one of the activities which will be carried on as a result of the passing of the legislation which will arise from this resolution will be a full scale attempt to find out not only what various groups of disabled can do, but exactly what jobs will be available in the economy of the 1970's and 1980's for these people.
The resolution ends with the suggestion that a national advisory council be set up. I think the Minister of Labour has already told us that this exists. I hope that sufficient professional personnel will be gathered in this national advisory council. I have the greatest admiration for those who work in the area of vocation rehabilitation, but sometimes I think we are overwhelmed by the cult of the amateur. I think helping the disabled is an area in which we need a great deal of professional assistance.
We took a great stride in our democratic system when we recognized that disabled people needed our help financially. We took another great stride when we realized that we should do everything in our power to help them lead a normal life. The third stride we must take on their behalf and on behalf of an even more efficient national economy is to remember that these people must have an opportunity to contribute to the fullest extent to the economy of the nation, thereby being able to contribute in a real way to the society in which they live.
I can assure the minister that this group will support these recommendations. We will support them in the hope that they will provide a more effective answer to the problem of vocational rehabilitation in Canada than we have today.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to say a few words about the resolution now before the house. This resolution is altogether necessary considering the needs of the disabled persons in our country, those who unfortunately, for some reason, are afflicted with a disease that prevents them from finding a job as easily as those enjoying perfect health.
There is surely nothing so distressing as the sight of a very intelligent and talented man or woman having difficulty in finding a job, only because employers are rather reluctant to employ a handicapped person without any formal training. This is why it is absolutely essential to give help to those who unfortunately, through some congenital condition or otherwise, are afflicted with a disability which prevents them from holding in life the position they deserve by their intelligence or other talents.
Vocational Rehabilitation
It is certain that for the morale of those people, it would be very useful to teach them a trade that would enable them to fill an important position within society. It is all the more important as those who will be disabled in the future, following an accident or for some other reason, will, upon entering this new phase in their life, find immediate comfort in the thought that others like themselves suffering from some disability have been able, by means of a trade they learned, to find a place for themselves in our modern life.
The provinces will be responsible for providing those rehabilitation courses, for giving the training that will enable the disabled persons and other outcasts of fortune to learn a trade. May I be permitted to suggest that those who will attend to this in the provinces consider what was done in this field in France, in England and more particularly in Germany.
It is common knowledge today that, as a result of the calamitous second world war, millions of civilians in Europe were wounded, during bombardments or following the invasion of European territories.
In Germany, especially, millions of citizens lost a limb or became paralysed, and this deprived post-war Germany of manpower which it certainly needed for its rehabilitation and reconstruction. But then the country had the good fortune of seeing a genius rise in its midst, Ludwig Erdhart, who gave his country an economic program which allowed it to recover and to attain the enviable position it enjoys today. Well, part of the program designed by Erdhart and his lieutenants was directed toward the rehabilitation of the disabled who could not as easily find jobs as those who, luckily, were in perfect health.
A rehabilitation and retraining program was put into operation, if I am not mistaken, more or less around 1947. Through this scheme, a very high percentage of the disabled civilians who were then unemployed are now usefully employed in the industries of their respective countries.
I think the provincial governments would be wise to send people to those European countries to study the programs which have been put to the test over the past 15 years; I am sure this could be very useful and would help us to improve the measure that is being put forward. Surely, this measure is of exceptional merit and will be supported by every hon. member in this house.

It has been my own fate to suffer a disability as a result of the war. I am thus in a position to state that on my return from the war, I took advantage of the rehabilitation services made available to me by the Department of Veterans Affairs and I was thus able, just as other war amputees of Canada, to adjust myself to a new kind of life.
